client:
I just can't seem to focus at work anymore. Every time I try to get something done, I suddenly remember my grandma's laugh or how she used to make my favorite soup when I was sick. It's been a month but it still feels so raw, like I should be "over it" by now but I'm not. 

I don't know if talking about it will help - won't it just make me feel worse? I keep thinking I should just push through and get back to normal, but then I feel guilty for trying to move on.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of pain and conflicting emotions about your grandma's passing—grief, nostalgia, and even some pressure about how you "should" be feeling. It’s okay to still feel raw; grief doesn’t follow a timeline. Would it be helpful to explore how you might honor her memory while also giving yourself permission to grieve in your own way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I guess I just don't know how to honor her memory without breaking down. Even seeing her favorite flowers at the grocery store makes my chest ache. Part of me wants to remember everything, but another part thinks maybe I should just avoid thinking about her so I can function at work. 

I've tried looking at old photos before and it just left me crying in my office for an hour. Doesn't that mean it's better to just try to move on?
therapist:
I notice you're speaking with a mix of tenderness and urgency—your words describe deep pain, but your tone carries almost a hopeful energy. It makes me wonder if part of you is already sensing that avoiding memories altogether might not be the kindest path, even though it feels overwhelming right now.  

What if there were small, gentle ways to remember her—maybe not photos yet, but something softer, like keeping one of her favorite flowers nearby or writing down a soup recipe? Grief isn’t all-or-nothing; we can find middle ground.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I do like the idea of something small and gentle—it feels less overwhelming than diving into old photos. But even keeping her favorite flower nearby feels risky. What if I look at it and start crying at work? I don’t want to fall apart in front of my coworkers. 

Maybe I could try writing down her soup recipe at home, though. It’s just hard to trust myself—what if I get stuck in that sadness again and can’t pull myself out?
therapist:
It’s clear you’re thinking deeply about how to balance honoring your grandma’s memory with protecting yourself in spaces like work—that’s such a thoughtful approach. Starting with something private, like writing down her recipe at home, feels like a safe first step.  

It’s okay if sadness comes up—it’s part of the process, and it doesn’t mean you’ll get stuck. What would it be like to trust yourself a little more to move through those moments, knowing the sadness will pass?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
I want to believe the sadness will pass, but it feels like such a heavy weight right now. Part of me worries that if I start writing down her recipes, I'll just end up missing her even more intensely. 

But maybe you're right that small steps could help. It's just hard to imagine feeling any better when everything still reminds me of her - even my kitchen smells like her cooking sometimes.
therapist:
It sounds like you’re holding onto both the weight of your grief and a glimmer of hope that small steps might help—that’s a brave place to be. Missing her intensely doesn’t mean you’re doing anything wrong; it’s a reflection of how much she meant to you.  

What if we think of this as a way to gently reconnect with her, rather than "fix" the sadness? How does it feel to imagine writing down one recipe, just as a way to keep her close, without expecting the grief to change right away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
That actually does sound comforting - thinking of it as reconnecting rather than fixing something broken. But I'm scared the recipe won't feel like enough, you know? Like it won't capture everything I miss about her. 

I still worry I'll just sit there staring at the page, crying over handwriting that isn't hers. Maybe I'm making this harder than it needs to be, but I don't want to do it wrong.
therapist:
There's such a deep care in your words—your love for her shines through even in this fear of not doing it "right." Grief isn't about perfect steps; it's about finding what feels meaningful to you, however small or imperfect.  

Would it help to think of the recipe as just one way to reconnect, with no pressure for it to hold everything you miss? Maybe it’s okay if tears come too—they’re part of honoring how much she meant to you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I never thought about tears being part of honoring her - that makes me feel less ashamed of crying when I think about her. But what if I start writing and suddenly realize I've forgotten some detail about how she made the soup? That thought terrifies me, like I'm losing her all over again when I can't remember perfectly. 

Maybe I should write down what I do remember first, even if it's incomplete. But it still feels so final, like putting her memory on paper means accepting she's really gone.
therapist:
I hear both courage and tenderness in your voice as you talk about this—it's clear how much care you're putting into preserving her memory. That fear of forgetting details makes so much sense; it’s not just about the recipe, but about wanting to hold onto her exactly as she was.  

What if we reframe this? Writing down what you remember isn’t about capturing everything perfectly—it’s about creating something that’s authentically yours, full of love and even the gaps that make it human. Could that feel a little gentler?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
That actually helps - thinking of the gaps as part of what makes it mine instead of mistakes. But I still feel this pressure to get it "right" before I start. What if I mess up the order of ingredients? She always said the secret was adding the garlic at just the right time... 

I think part of me wants this to be perfect because it might be the last new thing I'll ever "do" with her, if that makes sense. Like once I write it down, that's it - no more learning from her.
therapist:
I hear how meaningful this feels—like you're capturing something precious that connects you to her. It makes sense that you'd want it to be perfect, especially when it carries so much love and memory.  

What if we thought of the recipe not as an ending, but as something alive? You might surprise yourself—maybe years from now, you'll add your own twist to it, keeping her tradition growing in new ways. How does that idea sit with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
That actually makes my chest feel a little lighter - the idea that I could keep adding to it over time. But part of me rebels against changing anything about her recipe. Wouldn't that be disrespectful? 

Still...she was always experimenting in the kitchen, making little changes. Maybe she'd like knowing I'm carrying that forward. It just feels so strange to think about making it "mine" when it was always hers.
therapist:
It’s beautiful how much thought and care you’re putting into this—it’s clear how deeply you respect her and her traditions. Your grandma sounds like she loved creativity in the kitchen; experimenting might actually be a way to honor her spirit of joy and discovery.  

How does it feel to imagine her smiling at you adding your own touch, keeping her legacy alive in a way that feels true to both of you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
It feels comforting to imagine her smiling at me—she always encouraged me to try new things, even when I was scared. But I still feel hesitant, like I’m not ready to make changes to something so tied to her. 

What if I start by writing it down exactly as I remember it first, and maybe later, when it feels right, I can add my own twist? That way, I’m not rushing into changing something so important to me.
therapist:
That sounds like such a thoughtful approach—honoring her recipe exactly as you remember it first, while leaving room for your own creativity later when it feels right. It’s okay to take this step by step; there’s no rush to make changes.  

How does it feel to give yourself permission to do this at your own pace, knowing you can revisit it whenever you’re ready?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
It feels a little less overwhelming to take it step by step—like I don’t have to figure everything out at once. But I still worry that once I write it down, I’ll feel this pressure to keep it perfect, like a museum piece. 

What if I mess up the recipe later or forget something important? It feels like I’m trying to hold onto her in this one specific way, and I’m scared of losing even that.
therapist:
I hear how much love and care you're putting into this—it's clear how precious her memory is to you. While there's still some worry about "getting it right," I notice your voice has softened a bit as you talk about taking it step by step.  

What if we thought of the recipe as something that can evolve with you, just as your relationship with her did over time? It doesn't have to be perfect to be meaningful. How does that land for you?
